newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain truck driver union warns strike could worsen.
newsitem.headline: Spain truck driver union warns strike could worsen.

text.p: A strike by Spanish truck drivers demanding better labour conditions could worsen in coming days unless the government agrees to their demands, unions said on Wednesday.
By Wednesday, the week-long strike had spread to almost all of northern Spain with a large part of the country's 300,000 truck drivers out.
"To find a solution to this conflict, the Cabinet must meet and approve the measures we are asking for," said Jon Mikel Abellanal, spokesman for the Fedatrans union.
He warned there would be a "massive" clogging of Spain's roads and said the government must act speedily.
With hundreds of Spanish trucks blocking main roads, foreign drivers also found themselves caught up in the jam.
In the Catalan region, bordering France and Spain, 700 trucks were stalled on the roads.
On the French side of the border at Hendaye, around 100 French and foreign trucks were parked with drivers unwilling to enter Spain.
Blockages also spread to Portugal where local radio reported 300 Portuguese and foreign drivers stranded in the town of Vilar Formoso bordering Spain.
Unions said Spain's strike could soon freeze factory production for lack of raw materials and cut off food supplies in northern Spain.
In the Valladolid region, one of the worst affected areas, local media reported a number of manufacturers had halted production.
Police said on Wednesday the strike had turned violent in some areas.
In Leon province, a man was slightly injured when he was hit by a stone at a petrol station.
In Teruel, police arrested two pickets as they tried to stop a British lorry from passing and a further five were arrested for allegedly breaking the windows of another British truck near Pamplona.
Strikers are pushing for a restructuring of their sector including retirement at 60 years, instead of the current 65, and renegotiation of gasoline costs.

Last year, French truck drivers paralysed roads and disrupted much of Western Europe with a 12-day blockade forcing the French government to concede to a number of demands including retirement at 55 instead of 60.
The government said dialogue, not violence, was the answer to the sector's problems.

"It is absolutely vital that we sit down together at the negotiation table to resolve the problems in a sector which has many problems," Development Minister Rafael Arias Solgado told local radio on Wednesday.
